text: In an enzyme activity experiment, the statistical analysis produced p = 0.03. Which interpretation is best?
choices: The p-value shows the size of the biological effect, so a lower p-value always means a larger effect.
The p-value tells how likely the experiment is to be replicated exactly by another lab.
The p-value is the probability that the null hypothesis is true, so the null hypothesis has a probability of 0.03.
The difference is statistically significant at α = 0.05, so the null hypothesis is rejected.
explain: A p-value of 0.03 means that, if the null hypothesis were true, data at least this extreme would occur about 3% of the time. Because 0.03 is below 0.05, the difference is considered statistically significant at α = 0.05.
choice_explanations: Incorrect. Statistical significance and effect size are not the same thing. A tiny effect can have a small p-value if the data are precise enough.
Incorrect. Replication depends on many factors; the p-value is not a direct probability of exact replication.
Incorrect. A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true; it is the probability of getting data this extreme if the null hypothesis were true.
Correct. The key AP Biology decision is whether the p-value is below the chosen α level; if it is, reject the null hypothesis.

text: Four labs test whether a toxin lowers seed germination. Their p-values are 0.12, 0.08, 0.03, and 0.21. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: The largest p-value provides the strongest evidence because it is based on the greatest probability.
All of the p-values provide equally strong evidence because they were produced by hypothesis tests.
The lab with p = 0.03 provides the strongest statistical evidence against the null hypothesis.
Any p-value above 0 means the null hypothesis must be accepted.
explain: A smaller p-value means the observed data would be less likely if the null hypothesis were true. That does not by itself prove causation, but it does provide stronger statistical evidence against the null hypothesis than a larger p-value does.
choice_explanations: Incorrect. A large p-value means the data are more compatible with the null hypothesis, not less.
Incorrect. Hypothesis tests can produce very different strengths of evidence depending on the p-value.
Correct. Among comparable tests, the smallest p-value represents the data least consistent with the null hypothesis.
Incorrect. A positive p-value does not force acceptance of the null hypothesis; it may or may not be below α.

text: A student says, 'p = 0.04 means there is a 96% chance the treatment worked.' Which response is best?
choices: The student is incorrect because p = 0.04 refers to how unusual the data are if the null hypothesis is true, not the probability that the treatment worked.
A p-value above 0.05 proves that the null hypothesis is true.
A p-value only matters when there are more than two treatment groups.
The p-value directly measures the size of the biological effect, so the statement is acceptable if the effect seems small.
explain: P-values measure how compatible the data are with the null hypothesis. They do not directly tell you the probability that a hypothesis is true, the size of the effect, or whether an effect is biologically important.
choice_explanations: Correct. The best response correctly states what a p-value means and avoids overclaiming.
Incorrect. A large p-value means the data are compatible with the null hypothesis, not that the null hypothesis has been proven true.
Incorrect. P-values are relevant in many kinds of comparisons, including simple two-group comparisons.
Incorrect. Effect size and p-value are different ideas; a p-value does not quantify the size of the effect.

text: A result has p = 0.04. It is tested once at α = 0.05 and once at α = 0.01. Which statement is correct?
choices: The result is significant whenever the p-value is greater than α.
A result can only be significant if the p-value equals α exactly.
Changing α never changes the significance decision for the same data set.
The result is significant at α = 0.05 but not at α = 0.01.
explain: The decision rule is straightforward: reject the null hypothesis when p < α. If α becomes more lenient, some results that were previously non-significant can become significant, but only if the p-value falls below the new threshold.
choice_explanations: Incorrect. Significance requires p to be less than α, not greater than α.
Incorrect. The p-value does not have to equal α; it only needs to be below it.
Incorrect. The chosen α level absolutely can change whether a result is considered significant.
Correct. Significance depends on comparing the same p-value to the chosen α level.

text: Two experiments report the same p-value of 0.02, but one has a huge biological effect and the other a tiny effect. Which statement is best?
choices: If two tests have the same p-value, they must also have the same sample size and the same effect size.
The p-value alone does not tell you which experiment had the larger effect size.
The experiment with the lower mean must have had the smaller p-value, so the p-values cannot really be equal.
A p-value of 0.02 always means the treatment changed the response by exactly 2%.
explain: A p-value describes how incompatible the data are with the null hypothesis, not how large the effect is. Different experiments can reach the same p-value with different sample sizes, different variability, and very different effect sizes.
choice_explanations: Incorrect. P-values matter in both significant and non-significant results because they quantify compatibility with the null hypothesis.
Correct. This answer avoids one of the most common p-value misconceptions.
Incorrect. A p-value above 0.05 does not prove the null hypothesis; it only means the data were not strong enough to reject it.
Incorrect. Hypothesis testing does not mathematically prove either hypothesis true.

text: A researcher says, 'Because my result was not significant, I have shown the null hypothesis is correct.' Which critique is best?
choices: A non-significant result means the study did not provide enough evidence to reject the null hypothesis; it does not prove the null hypothesis is correct.
The claim is fine because significance testing is designed to prove one of the two hypotheses is true.
The claim is fine because any p-value above 0.05 proves the null hypothesis.
The critique is wrong because p-values are only used when the result is significant.
explain: Hypothesis tests are asymmetric: they can provide evidence against the null hypothesis, but failing to reject the null does not prove it true. The study may simply lack enough evidence, power, or precision.
choice_explanations: Correct. This answer avoids one of the most common p-value misconceptions.
Incorrect. Hypothesis testing does not mathematically prove either hypothesis true.
Incorrect. A p-value above 0.05 does not prove the null hypothesis; it only means the data were not strong enough to reject it.
Incorrect. P-values matter in both significant and non-significant results because they quantify compatibility with the null hypothesis.

text: A study finds p = 0.048 for a very small difference in mean chlorophyll concentration. Which statement is best?
choices: Because the p-value is close to 0.05, the result should automatically be treated as biologically trivial.
The p-value proves the treatment changed chlorophyll concentration by 4.8%.
The difference is statistically significant at α = 0.05, but the p-value alone does not tell whether the effect is biologically large or important.
A p-value below 0.05 means there is less than a 5% chance that any measurement error occurred.
explain: A p-value below 0.05 supports rejecting the null hypothesis, but it says nothing by itself about effect size or biological importance. A statistically significant result can still represent a small effect.
choice_explanations: Incorrect. This either confuses p-value with biological importance or reverses the effect of variability.
Incorrect. Equal mean differences do not guarantee equal p-values because variability and sample size matter too.
Correct. This answer uses the p-value properly without confusing it with effect size, error rate, or proof.
Incorrect. P-values are directly affected by variability and can absolutely be calculated in such experiments.

text: Two versions of the same experiment give the same mean difference, but Experiment 1 has very low variability and Experiment 2 has very high variability. Which experiment is more likely to produce the smaller p-value?
choices: Both experiments must have the same p-value because the mean difference is the same.
Experiment 2, because higher variability always forces the p-value downward.
Experiment 1, because lower variability makes the same mean difference easier to detect statistically.
Neither experiment can have a p-value because variability and p-values are unrelated.
explain: With the same mean difference, lower variability makes the signal clearer relative to the noise. That usually leads to stronger statistical evidence and therefore a smaller p-value.
